title: How Can Importers Plan Carton Packing for Custom Water Bottles Before Export?
description: A practical B2B guide to custom water bottle export packing, carton dimensions, labels, 3PL receiving, freight planning and reorder control.
intro: Export packing is easy to underestimate because a quotation usually starts with a bottle and ends with a unit price. Importers, distributors and 3PL teams need the complete path from the approved sample to the receiving dock: individual protection, carton quantity, outer dimensions, labels, pallet assumptions and destination handling. This guide explains how to plan that path before a custom water bottle order is released.
coverAlt: Illustrative export warehouse scene with packed reusable bottles and cartons; contextual image only, not an XUYI shipment, customer or factory record.
primary_keyword: custom water bottle export carton packing planning

sections.heading: 1. Begin with the receiving channel and sales plan
sections.paragraph: Carton planning should start with where the finished bottles will go, not with a generic promise of export packaging. Tell the supplier whether the goods will arrive at your own warehouse, a 3PL, a retail distribution centre, a marketplace fulfilment site or several country-level locations. Explain whether the order will be sold as single units, colour assortments, case packs or promotional kits. A small distributor may need mixed cartons with readable labels, while a large retailer may require a fixed case quantity and a booking-compatible pallet. Write the destination, receiving rules, expected order split and first delivery window into the purchasing brief. This gives the manufacturer a reason to discuss carton quantity and dimensions early, before printed packaging and freight are already committed.

sections.heading: 2. Select the bottle and capacity with the carton in mind
sections.paragraph: A bottle that looks compact in a catalogue can become difficult to pack when the lid, carry loop, sleeve or individual box is added. Confirm the assembled height, widest point, lid projection and any parts that can press against neighbouring units. XUYI model 2502 is listed at 750ml; use that catalogue value as a starting reference, then ask for a physical sample and actual packed dimensions before fixing a case count. If two capacities are being compared, request separate carton calculations rather than assuming a larger bottle simply reduces the number of units proportionally. Test one complete packed unit, one inner bundle and one master carton. The purpose is to balance protection, cube, handling weight and the receiving channel's shelf or conveyor constraints.

sections.heading: 3. Request a carton data sheet that logistics can actually use
sections.paragraph: For every approved model and colour split, ask for units per master carton, carton length, width, height, gross weight, net weight and the packing arrangement. Request the data in one consistent unit system and keep the original supplier assumptions beside any internal conversion. XUYI model 2505 is listed at 800ml, but capacity alone does not tell a freight forwarder how much space the shipment will occupy. The carton data must reflect the final lid, decoration, individual bag or box and any inserts. Ask whether cartons can be mixed by colour, how mixed cartons are counted and whether a separate SKU label is required. Do not build a freight budget from a catalogue photograph or from a carton size copied from another bottle.

sections.heading: 4. Protect the decorated bottle without hiding the packing cost
sections.paragraph: Custom printing and colour matching add a practical packing question: what may rub, bend, crush or transfer during transit? Ask whether the printed surface needs a bag, divider, sleeve, tissue, inner box or another protection method. For a large format such as XUYI model 2305, listed at 1600ml, compare the space and protection required for the bottle, lid and handle instead of copying a compact bottle's inner pack. Request a packing sample or a clear packing drawing when the order is sensitive to scratches, print alignment or mixed components. Make the protection cost visible in the quotation. A slightly higher pack cost can be cheaper than receiving decorated bottles with scuffed surfaces, loose lids or cartons that cannot be safely stacked.

sections.heading: 5. Align carton labels with the 3PL and retail system
sections.paragraph: A carton label is useful only when the receiving team knows how to read it. Confirm which fields are required: model or SKU, colour, capacity, units per carton, purchase order, destination, carton sequence and barcode if applicable. Ask the 3PL whether labels must be placed on two sides, whether mixed cartons need a special mark and whether the warehouse scans the outer carton or each inner unit. Keep the language and symbols consistent with the purchase order and commercial invoice. If a private-label buyer has different labels for several channels, separate the label artwork and approval records by shipment rather than hiding all variations under one generic file. A simple label specification prevents cartons from being opened just to identify their contents.

sections.heading: 6. Calculate freight and landed cost from approved packing data
sections.paragraph: Once the sample and carton data are confirmed, compare freight scenarios using the same shipment assumptions. Include the number of cartons, gross weight, volume, pallet or floor-loaded plan, destination charges, customs responsibilities and any required delivery appointment. Ask whether the carton dimensions are measured after the final packaging is assembled and whether the quoted pack supports the planned transport. Avoid treating a unit price as a landed cost. If a supplier recommends a new carton quantity, update the freight calculation and the warehouse receiving plan at the same time. A cost table should show the source data and mark estimates clearly, so a buyer can see which figures need confirmation before booking the export shipment.

sections.heading: 7. Lock the packing file before production and preserve it for reorders
sections.paragraph: Before production starts, attach the approved sample photos, carton drawing, label artwork, packing quantity, inspection points and shipment instructions to the purchase order. Name one person who can approve a change and record the version number when a bottle colour, lid, insert or carton is revised. At pre-shipment inspection, open representative cartons and verify the actual inner pack, label, count and visible decoration against the approved file. After arrival, record damage, missing units, mislabelled cartons and 3PL feedback by model and colour. This creates a reliable reorder record. A future supplier or colleague should be able to see why the case pack was chosen and which packing change would require a new freight calculation.

checklist: Identify the warehouse, 3PL, retailer or fulfilment channel before fixing the pack.
Confirm assembled bottle dimensions, lid projection and packed sample fit.
Request units per carton, dimensions, weights and packing arrangement in writing.
Calculate separate case packs for different capacities or colour assortments.
Protect printed surfaces with a reviewed inner-pack solution.
Define carton label fields, placement, barcode and mixed-carton rules.
Compare freight using approved carton count, cube and gross weight.
Mark estimated logistics figures separately from confirmed supplier data.
Attach the carton drawing and label proof to the purchase order.
Record receiving damage and packing lessons for the next reorder.

faqs.question: What carton information does an importer need from a bottle supplier?
faqs.answer: Request units per carton, inner-pack arrangement, carton dimensions, gross and net weight, colour or SKU split, label fields and any pallet assumptions. Confirm the figures after final packaging is approved.

faqs.question: Should every water bottle capacity have its own carton plan?
faqs.answer: Usually it should be checked separately. Different heights, lids, handles and individual packs can change the safe case quantity and the shipment cube even when the bottle family looks similar.

faqs.question: How do I prepare custom bottle cartons for a 3PL?
faqs.answer: Ask the 3PL for label placement and barcode rules, then align model, colour, capacity, case quantity, purchase order and carton sequence fields with the supplier's packing file.

faqs.question: Can export packing be changed after a sample is approved?
faqs.answer: It can be discussed, but any change to inner protection, carton quantity, dimensions or labels should be recorded, re-costed and approved before production so freight and receiving assumptions remain accurate.

title: Which Logo Printing and Branding Method Should You Choose for Custom Water Bottles in Bulk?
description: A practical B2B guide to choosing a logo printing and branding method for bulk water bottles by surface, artwork, quantity, use case, sample proof and reorder control.
intro: Start by describing where the bottle will be used and what the logo must communicate. A one-color mark on a smooth body, a multi-color event graphic, a small mark on a lid and a retail-ready package may need different decisions. Write down the recipient, expected handling, cleaning expectations, outdoor exposure, destination market and whether the bottle will be sold or distributed. Then identify the actual surfaces: body, lid, strap, sleeve, carton or label. The same artwork can look balanced on a 500ml-class bottle and crowded on a smaller panel. A useful RFQ asks the supplier to recommend a method for the exact model while keeping the buyer responsible for visual approval. This prevents a generic logo-available answer from being mistaken for a complete decoration specification.
coverAlt: Natural product photograph of branded reusable bottles and logo samples for a bulk custom water bottle order; confirm the exact method on the selected sample.
group: Custom Bottle Branding and Logo Sourcing
primary_keyword: custom water bottle logo printing methods for bulk orders

sections.heading: 1. Start with the use case, surface and brand result
sections.paragraph: Start by describing where the bottle will be used and what the logo must communicate. A one-color mark on a smooth body, a multi-color event graphic, a small mark on a lid and a retail-ready package may need different decisions. Write down the recipient, expected handling, cleaning expectations, outdoor exposure, destination market and whether the bottle will be sold or distributed. Then identify the actual surfaces: body, lid, strap, sleeve, carton or label. The same artwork can look balanced on a 500ml-class bottle and crowded on a smaller panel. A useful RFQ asks the supplier to recommend a method for the exact model while keeping the buyer responsible for visual approval. This prevents a generic logo-available answer from being mistaken for a complete decoration specification.

sections.heading: 2. Compare decoration methods as a buyer decision
sections.paragraph: Ask the supplier to separate available decoration routes instead of putting every logo request into one vague line. Direct print may suit a defined artwork area, while a transfer, label or sleeve may be considered when the design needs more coverage; laser or another finish should be discussed only if the exact surface and material support it. Packaging print is a separate branding layer and is not proof that the bottle body can carry the same result. For each option, collect printable area, color limitations, setup or tooling charge, proof format, sample timing, minimum quantity and reorder reference. Do not assume that a method used on one material or shape transfers to another. The useful comparison is the complete approval path, not a list of technique names.

sections.heading: 3. Give artwork instructions that a factory can use
sections.paragraph: Send a clean artwork package with an editable vector file where available, a raster preview for visual comparison, intended colors, maximum print area, preferred orientation and the brand owner’s approval contact. Mark which colors are essential and which can be approximated only after a physical proof. Include a dimensioned placement sketch when the logo must align with a handle, seam, measurement mark or lid feature. Ask the supplier to return a proof showing the logo on the actual bottle outline, not only on a blank rectangle. If the artwork contains fine lines, small text, gradients or several colors, ask what can be held consistently at the proposed size. A dated artwork version and dated proof reduce the chance that a late email attachment becomes the untracked production file.

sections.heading: 4. Treat the decorated sample as the approval gate
sections.paragraph: A decorated sample should answer more than whether the logo is visible. Compare position, scale, orientation, edge quality, color appearance, contrast, adhesion or finish as appropriate to the method, and the way the logo sits beside the lid and other molded features. Handle and clean the sample according to the intended use where safe and relevant, while recording what was actually tested rather than promising a universal durability result. Check the assembled bottle because a cap or strap can change the visual center after production. Keep photos of the approved sample beside the model number, artwork version and packaging instruction. If a supplier offers only a digital mockup, mark the order as pending physical decoration approval.

sections.heading: 5. Compare quote lines without hiding branding costs
sections.paragraph: Request a quote that separates bottle, decoration, artwork setup, sample, packaging print, labels, individual packing, master carton and freight assumptions. Ask whether the price changes with one color versus multiple colors, one position versus several, a split color order or revised artwork. A low unit price can be misleading when setup, proofing or printed packaging appears later as an unlisted charge. Put the quantity tier and destination on the same comparison sheet and record which items are estimates. If evaluating XUYI model 2501 at its listed 550ml capacity or model 2502 at 750ml, treat catalogue data as a reference and confirm the exact decoration area, component set and carton plan before comparing offers.

sections.heading: 6. Build quality checks around brand risk
sections.paragraph: Brand damage often comes from small inconsistencies that were never included in the inspection plan: an artwork version changed, a logo placed too close to a seam, a color judged under different light, a lid hiding part of the mark, or cartons mixed between variants. Write inspection points for model, capacity, body color, lid color, logo artwork version, position, orientation, visible defects, packing and carton labels. Define what evidence is required before release, such as first-unit photos, a production sample or a report tied to the purchase order. Keep material or compliance requests separate from decoration approval; a printed logo is not evidence that the finished assembly meets a destination requirement.

sections.heading: 7. Choose the method that can survive a reorder
sections.paragraph: The best decoration method fits the current use case and can be repeated with controlled instructions. Save the final model, surface, artwork file name, color reference, placement dimensions, proof image, approved sample photos, packing instruction and change history. Ask what would force a new proof: body, material, lid, artwork, color split or market change. For a distributor or private-label buyer, this record is more valuable than a one-time promise because it lets the next team request the same result without guessing. If the program may expand to another capacity, approve each shape separately rather than assuming the logo scales automatically. A short documented approval path turns custom branding into a reliable B2B product line.

checklist: Define the audience, use case, destination and buying decision before requesting a quote.
Record the exact model, listed capacity and component assumptions in the RFQ.
Request a complete physical sample before approving decoration, closure or packing.
Separate catalogue facts from custom material, compliance and performance inquiries.
Compare quantity, color, logo, packing, carton and freight assumptions together.
Keep artwork, sample photos and test notes with the model record.
Define who approves changes to the body, lid, seal, logo and carton.
Use a dated inspection or test record tied to the exact assembled sample.

title: Which Water Bottle Closure Type Is Best for a Wholesale Sourcing Order?
description: A buyer-friendly B2B guide to choosing a water bottle closure type for wholesale by use case, neck compatibility, cleaning, leak testing, branding and reorder control.
intro: Start with the person who will use the bottle and the moment when they will open it. A gym user, a school program, a commuter, a warehouse team and a retail customer may value different combinations of one-hand access, spill control, cleaning access and carrying convenience. State whether the bottle will be used at a desk, outdoors, in a bag, during exercise or in a child-focused program. Also record whether the buyer needs a wide opening, a straw, a handle, a lock or a simple screw closure. These are requirements to confirm, not automatic performance claims. Once the use case is clear, the supplier can recommend a closure family and the buyer can test the full assembled sample instead of comparing isolated cap photographs.
coverAlt: Natural product photograph of bottle lids, seals and straw components for a wholesale sourcing decision; confirm fit, material and testing on the selected model.
group: Wholesale Bottle Closure and Cap Selection
primary_keyword: best water bottle closure type for wholesale order
secondary_keywords: leak test checklist for reusable bottles

sections.heading: 1. Answer the use-case question before naming a cap
sections.paragraph: Start with the person who will use the bottle and the moment when they will open it. A gym user, a school program, a commuter, a warehouse team and a retail customer may value different combinations of one-hand access, spill control, cleaning access and carrying convenience. State whether the bottle will be used at a desk, outdoors, in a bag, during exercise or in a child-focused program. Also record whether the buyer needs a wide opening, a straw, a handle, a lock or a simple screw closure. These are requirements to confirm, not automatic performance claims. Once the use case is clear, the supplier can recommend a closure family and the buyer can test the full assembled sample instead of comparing isolated cap photographs.

sections.heading: 2. Compare flip, straw, screw and sport closure families
sections.paragraph: A flip closure may be convenient for quick access, a straw route may suit a particular drinking posture, a screw closure may be valued for simple parts, and a sport-style top may be requested for active use. An auto-seal or lock feature adds another approval question rather than removing the need for one. Use these labels as starting points only: suppliers may use different names for similar-looking designs, and the same family can have different threads, seals, buttons and removable pieces. Ask for the exact assembly drawing or complete sample, listed materials, cleaning path, open and closed position and intended handling. A comparison is useful when it records what was seen and tested, not when it turns a cap name into an unsupported promise.

sections.heading: 3. Confirm neck finish, thread and seal compatibility
sections.paragraph: The cap is not an interchangeable accessory unless the neck, thread, sealing surface and component dimensions are compatible. For each proposed model, record the bottle body, neck finish, cap version, gasket or seal, vent or straw parts and any lock or hinge. Request a complete assembled sample and check that the cap closes without cross-threading, the seal sits evenly, the lid does not interfere with the body and removable pieces can be handled as intended. If a buyer wants one cap on several capacities or shapes, test every body rather than assuming the same thread guarantees the same user result. This matters when a catalogue contains multiple plastic sports bottle capacities. Fit is a product fact to verify on the selected SKU.

sections.heading: 4. Create a practical leak and handling test plan
sections.paragraph: Do not replace a test plan with the word leakproof. Define the liquid, fill level, orientation, time, temperature, opening cycles and movement that represent the intended use, then record the result and exact assembled sample. Check the closed bottle in a bag or carton position where relevant, and separately observe opening action, lock position, straw or spout access and cleaning steps. If the product is for children or a public program, add handling supervision and cleaning instructions to the buyer brief rather than making a broad safety claim. Ask what was tested, on which model and with which cap version. Evidence is stronger when tied to a dated sample and purchase-order specification.

sections.heading: 5. Match closure complexity to the audience and service plan
sections.paragraph: More parts can create more questions for cleaning, spare components, assembly and after-sales handling. A school or employee program may prefer an easy-to-understand closure, while a retail or sports line may accept a more feature-rich design if packaging and instructions explain it. Ask how the supplier identifies replacement caps, gaskets, straws or locks and whether the carton can keep variants separated. Confirm the exact color split and whether cap color is part of the bottle SKU or a separate component instruction. XUYI model 2095 is listed at 500ml and model 2106 at 750ml; use those catalogue facts only as references while confirming the full cap/body assembly and intended audience.

sections.heading: 6. Put closure questions into the RFQ and sample record
sections.paragraph: A useful closure RFQ names the bottle model or shape, capacity, neck or thread reference if known, closure family, material direction, color, logo location, packing, quantity and destination. Add questions about removable parts, cleaning access, spare parts, sample timing, leak or handling test scope and change control. Ask the supplier to mark what is confirmed and what depends on a physical sample. Save the cap drawing, sample photos, approval notes and any test record with the purchase order. If the buyer later changes from a screw lid to a straw or flip design, treat it as a new configuration with a new cost and approval review. Put the approved cap version, body reference and test condition on the same purchase-order line so a later replacement part cannot silently change the assembly. This small record also gives quality and warehouse teams a clear way to identify the correct carton.

sections.heading: 7. Select the closure that can be repeated, cleaned and explained
sections.paragraph: The final choice should be easy for a purchasing team to explain: this closure matches the users, fits the selected body, passed the agreed checks, has clear packing and can be identified at reorder. Keep a one-page closure specification with photos of open and closed positions, model, capacity, component list, cleaning notes and test evidence. Record what the test did not cover. When a future order changes capacity, material, color or closure component, compare it against the approved reference and decide whether a new sample is required. A reliable wholesale closure decision is not a universal ranking; it is a documented match between the buyer’s use case and an exact repeatable assembly.

Record the exact model, listed capacity and component assumptions in the RFQ.

title: What Water Bottle Capacity Should a Corporate Wellness Program Order in Bulk?
description: A practical B2B guide to choosing 500ml, 750ml or larger water bottle capacity for a corporate wellness program, with fit, refill, packing and reorder checks.
intro: Ask what the program is trying to support and where the bottle will be carried. A desk giveaway, a commuting kit, a warehouse hydration program, a sports event and a retail-style employee benefit can have different capacity priorities. Write down recipient groups, refill access, expected carry distance, bag or cup-holder limits, event duration, decoration area and whether the bottle is a daily item or a campaign gift. The goal is not to prescribe medical intake or promise behavior change. It is to select a physical product people can carry, use and recognize. A written behavior brief lets purchasing compare 500ml, 750ml and larger options on the same assumptions instead of choosing from a product photo.
coverAlt: Natural product photograph comparing 500ml, 750ml and 1L-class bottles for corporate wellness procurement; confirm exact model dimensions and packing before ordering.
primary_keyword: corporate wellness water bottle capacity bulk order

sections.heading: 1. Start with the program behavior, not the biggest number
sections.paragraph: Ask what the program is trying to support and where the bottle will be carried. A desk giveaway, a commuting kit, a warehouse hydration program, a sports event and a retail-style employee benefit can have different capacity priorities. Write down recipient groups, refill access, expected carry distance, bag or cup-holder limits, event duration, decoration area and whether the bottle is a daily item or a campaign gift. The goal is not to prescribe medical intake or promise behavior change. It is to select a physical product people can carry, use and recognize. A written behavior brief lets purchasing compare 500ml, 750ml and larger options on the same assumptions instead of choosing from a product photo.

sections.heading: 2. Compare 500ml, 750ml and 1L-class options as trade-offs
sections.paragraph: A 500ml bottle is a compact class, roughly a 17 US fl oz class reference; 750ml is roughly a 25 US fl oz class; and 1000ml is roughly a 32 US fl oz class. These are approximate communication aids, not a substitute for listed metric capacity or exact filled dimensions. The smaller class may be easier to carry and pack, while the middle class can reduce refill frequency without the physical footprint of a larger jug. A 1L-class choice may suit a long session but can affect weight, bag fit, carton quantity and handling. Put metric capacity, approximate ounce class, actual height and diameter, filled weight and use-case notes in one comparison sheet so the internal decision is transparent.

sections.heading: 3. Test recipient fit before approving the program size
sections.paragraph: The right capacity is partly a fit question. Place the assembled sample in bags, desk spaces, vehicle holders, lockers or event kits that represent the audience. Record height, diameter, cap projection, handle clearance, filled weight and whether the bottle can be opened without interfering with nearby items. Ask a small internal group to handle each candidate and record practical comments, but do not turn a small trial into a universal market claim. If the program has several recipient groups, a two-size range may be more useful than forcing every person into one capacity; if it uses one SKU for simplicity, document the reason. Confirm model and listed capacity before artwork, carton labels and purchase-order release.

sections.heading: 4. Link capacity to refill, packing and landed-cost assumptions
sections.paragraph: Capacity changes more than the number printed on a product page. It can affect body dimensions, filled weight, units per carton, protective material, shelf or kit space and freight calculation. Ask for exact carton dimensions, gross weight, units per carton, individual packing and destination assumptions for each candidate. Do not invent a freight saving from a smaller bottle or a productivity benefit from a larger one; calculate with confirmed packing data and the buyer’s route. If comparing XUYI model 2095 at 500ml, model 2502 at 750ml or model 2505 at 800ml, keep model, material, lid, color split and carton configuration visible in the same cost file.

sections.heading: 5. Decide whether one size or a small range is easier to maintain
sections.paragraph: One capacity can simplify artwork, purchase orders, storage, internal distribution and reorder control. A small range can improve fit for different teams, but creates more SKU, color, carton and sample decisions. Ask whether the program manager can keep variants separated and whether employees understand the difference. Confirm whether the logo area scales across models and whether the same lid, packing label or instruction can be used. If a size change is proposed after artwork approval, treat it as a new product configuration until body, capacity, decoration and carton plan are checked. The best program size is the one the organization can distribute and reorder without hidden operational work.

sections.heading: 6. Approve capacity with a complete model record
sections.paragraph: Before releasing a bulk order, save the product model, listed metric capacity, approximate ounce class used in marketing, measured dimensions, filled handling note, material direction, lid version, color split, logo proof, individual packing and master-carton data. Mark which values are catalogue references and which were measured or confirmed on the sample. Ask the supplier to identify any tolerance or component change that would require a new approval. Keep the capacity decision separate from claims about hydration, health or performance; a bottle size is a product attribute, not a guaranteed outcome. This record lets the wellness lead, buyer and warehouse team work from the same version and gives the next reorder a clear reference point.

sections.heading: 7. Use a simple decision rule for the final bulk order
sections.paragraph: Choose the capacity that passes four questions: can the intended recipient carry it, can the program explain and distribute it, can the packing and landed-cost plan support it, and can the supplier reproduce the exact configuration? If one answer is no, return to the sample or comparison sheet instead of compensating with marketing language. A 500ml, 750ml or 1L-class option can all be reasonable in different programs. The defensible decision is supported by recipient fit, actual dimensions, metric capacity, approximate ounce communication, carton evidence and an approved model record. That is more useful to a procurement team than a generic claim that one size is always best.

title: How Can a Retail Buyer Build a Reusable Water Bottle Assortment for a First Wholesale Order?
description: A practical wholesale assortment plan for specialty retailers: match bottle size classes, colors, SKU data and reorder rules to real shelf demand.
intro: A first bottle order is easier to manage when every SKU has a clear shelf role. Start with who shops your store, what they use the bottle for and how they compare sizes and colors. Then ask the manufacturer for model-level samples, confirmed specifications and reorder data before you divide quantities.
coverAlt: A person holds a clear reusable water bottle outdoors under a bright sky, showing its everyday carry form; contextual Pexels photo, not an XUYI product or customer.
primary_keyword: wholesale reusable water bottle assortment for retail buyers
secondary_keywords: wholesale bottle buying checklist for retailers
water bottle size and color SKU planning
custom bottle manufacturer for retail assortment

sections.heading: 1. Define the shelf job before choosing models
sections.paragraph: Before asking a factory for a catalog, write down the customer and the decision the shelf must support. A campus shop, outdoor retailer, museum store and general gift shop may all sell reusable bottles, but their buyers do not necessarily compare the same carry needs, colors, size classes or price points. Use actual sales records, customer questions and the neighboring products on the shelf to define the role of each item. If this is a new category with no history, mark assumptions as assumptions and start with a small, measurable assortment plan rather than claiming a proven demand curve. Give the manufacturer the intended channel, target user, destination market and planned retail presentation so the sample review answers the right question. A bottle that looks attractive in a supplier photo still needs a clear reason to earn a SKU slot.

sections.heading: 2. Build a size ladder with a purpose for each option
sections.paragraph: Do not add several capacities simply because they appear in a catalog. Decide what job each size class serves, then compare the actual milliliter capacity, outside dimensions and filled weight from the specific model record. XUYI model 2400 is listed at 380 ml, model 2401 at 650 ml and model 2470 at 800 ml; their product pages also show approximate oz size classes, not exact fluid-ounce conversions. These records can help a buyer compare compact and larger choices, but they do not prove that all three fit every store or user. Ask for assembled samples and measure them beside the shelf depth, gift bag or customer carry use you actually sell. Keep exact ml as the specification and treat any oz wording as an approximate market class.

sections.heading: 3. Choose colors shoppers can identify and you can reorder
sections.paragraph: A color plan should be readable at the shelf and usable in a purchase order. Select core colors from the store’s customer and brand context, then decide whether seasonal colors are a limited test or a standing SKU. Ask the factory how each color is identified, what reference or physical sample will be used, and whether the color applies to the body, lid, strap or another component. Do not assume a screen image, informal color name or nearby product is a binding match. Record one approved reference for each component and name who signs off. If the assortment contains several colors, list a separate SKU row for each sellable combination so the buyer can connect photos, stock counts, carton labels and reorders without guessing which color was approved.

sections.heading: 4. Separate model, lid and body combinations in the SKU map
sections.paragraph: A useful assortment file distinguishes the bottle model from the combinations the retailer will actually order. Give every line a model identifier, stated capacity in ml, color, lid or accessory configuration, material information exactly as confirmed, decoration status, packaging unit and destination. If the manufacturer says an option is customizable, keep it marked as a request until the selected sample and order documents confirm it. This prevents a custom color or component discussed in email from silently becoming a catalog fact. Review the full combination with the supplier: the approved body, lid, strap, artwork and package should refer to the same model revision. Use the current Model 2400 page as one comparison record, then check the product page and physical sample before treating it as a final SKU.

sections.heading: 5. Allocate a first order using evidence, not a copied split
sections.paragraph: Quantity allocation should come from the buyer’s channel, shelf capacity, purchasing budget, forecast confidence and the supplier’s written order conditions. Ask for the minimum order quantity by model, color and decoration method rather than assuming one factory-wide MOQ. Identify launch priorities, controlled test variants and items that should wait until sales data arrives. Put total and per-variant quantities in one table; otherwise a quote may hide an unworkable split. If there is no sales history, keep that uncertainty visible and agree how the retailer will review sell-through after stock arrives. Never claim a mix is proven without actual records. A useful quote lets the buyer compare the same model, packing basis, destination and quantity tier across suppliers.

sections.heading: 6. Keep product identifiers and artwork tied to each variant
sections.paragraph: Retail readiness includes a data handoff, not just a bottle and logo. Prepare a master record connecting model, sellable color and capacity combination, internal SKU, barcode or GTIN status, image, package artwork and approved sample. GS1 explains that distinct product variants can require distinct GTINs; confirm the brand owner’s assignment and trading-partner rules before printing labels. Do not reuse a barcode because two bottles look similar, and do not print a number before the exact variant and responsible brand owner are confirmed. For another size reference, compare Model 2401 against its current page and keep its capacity, color and artwork record separate from other models.

sections.heading: 7. Approve the range once, then make reorders repeatable
sections.paragraph: Before production, review one assortment approval sheet with the buyer and supplier. It should show chosen model, confirmed capacity, component colors, approved decoration, package, quantity by sellable variant, label or barcode owner, destination and sample reference. Save dated sample photos beside the specification file, and record open questions as holds rather than leaving them in chat. On reorder, compare the quote against that approved version and ask the supplier to identify every proposed change. Model 2470 can serve as another current catalog reference, but a product page is not a substitute for the specific sample and order confirmation. Version control makes the first order easier to evaluate and the next one easier to reproduce.

checklist: Define the store type, shopper and job for each SKU.
Record exact model and ml; mark oz as an approximate size class.
Check sample dimensions against the real shelf, bag or carry use.
List colors separately and identify the approved reference per component.
Confirm lid, strap, material and customization for the selected model.
Ask MOQ and price by model, color and decoration combination.
Separate launch priorities from low-confidence test variants.
Confirm GTIN/barcode owner before label printing.
Match images and package artwork to the approved variant.
Save sample approval, quantity split and reorder revision together.

faqs.question: How many bottle models should a retailer include in a first wholesale order?
faqs.answer: There is no universal count. Choose models with a defined shelf role that can be sampled and ordered in workable quantities. Use store data where available and label assumptions when the category is new.

faqs.question: Should a buyer list both ml and oz on the purchase sheet?
faqs.answer: Keep the manufacturer's stated milliliter capacity as the exact specification. If an oz size class helps the target market, label it approximate and confirm the conversion convention instead of presenting an exact equality.

faqs.question: Can one barcode be used for a bottle in several colors?
faqs.answer: Do not assume so. Check the brand owner's GTIN assignment and retailer requirements for each sellable variant before labels are printed. Identify every approved color and capacity combination in the SKU file.

faqs.question: What should a bottle manufacturer confirm before quoting an assortment?
faqs.answer: Send model, exact capacity, color and lid request, decoration, pack format, quantity by variant and destination. Ask the manufacturer to separate confirmed SKU facts from options that still require a sample or approval.

title: What Should Sports Retail Buyers Test Before Reordering Reusable Water Bottles in Bulk?
description: A sports-retail sample checklist covering cap handling, leak checks, carry fit, cleaning, capacity and reorder control before a wholesale purchase.
intro: A product photo cannot answer whether a bottle suits a real customer or training routine. Before repeating a bulk order, evaluate an assembled sample in the way shoppers will carry, open, refill and clean it, then record the exact conditions and approved model.
coverAlt: Hands open a reusable bottle outdoors; contextual stock photography, not a verified XUYI model, customer or performance test.
primary_keyword: sports retailer reusable water bottle sample testing before bulk reorder

sections.heading: 1. Define the activity and test conditions first
sections.paragraph: A sample test is useful only when the buyer states what the customer will actually do. A trail shop, gym, cycling retailer and team dealer may have different carry methods, refill points and cleaning routines. Write down the intended activity, who will handle the bottle, what bag or holder it must fit, how often it will be opened and what the retailer plans to say on its product page. Keep the test limited to the selected SKU and ordinary use described by the manufacturer. Do not turn an informal store check into a laboratory claim or a blanket leak-proof guarantee. Record date, sample model, cap and body combination, reviewer and steps taken. This makes the result useful for a reorder decision and prevents a different variant from inheriting approval it never received.

sections.heading: 2. Open and close the actual cap with the intended user
sections.paragraph: Use the assembled sample rather than a loose cap from another model. Have the intended reviewer open and close it several times with dry hands, then repeat only handling conditions relevant to customers, such as sport gloves if they are part of the use case. Note whether grip, direction, parts and closure sequence are clear; do not assume a photo demonstrates one-handed use. If a removable part or seal needs a separate cleaning step, write it down and ask the supplier for model-specific care instructions. XUYI pages for models 2400, 2401 and 2470 identify separate product models; a buyer should verify each cap and assembled sample before treating them as interchangeable.

sections.heading: 3. Run a controlled leak check and document what it proves
sections.paragraph: If the retail team performs a leak check, define the method before testing: fill level, closure procedure, wait time, orientation, transport container and inspection point. Use a safe water-only sample and follow manufacturer instructions. Photograph the setup and record the result for that sample under those conditions. A pass on one assembled sample does not establish every production unit's performance, prove suitability for hot liquids or guarantee use in every bag position. If a customer requires a particular standard, ask what test method and evidence apply to the exact SKU and market. Treat a failed or ambiguous result as a hold: check the closure assembly, ask the supplier for clarification and retest a corrected sample rather than changing the requirement afterward.

sections.heading: 4. Check carrying fit against the real retail use
sections.paragraph: The bottle must fit the way the target customer will carry it. Measure the sample's widest outside dimension and height, then compare it with the relevant cycle cage, backpack pocket, gym bag, counter display or team kit. Test with the intended strap or accessory fitted if the selected variant includes one. Record whether the bottle can be inserted and removed without interference, but avoid claiming universal compatibility from one equipment item. Ask the manufacturer for exact dimensions for the model and revision; use a sample to resolve tolerances and protruding cap features. A useful sports assortment may contain different capacity classes, but every option should have a defined user need rather than simply increasing the catalog lines.

sections.heading: 5. Review cleaning and care as part of the buying decision
sections.paragraph: A sport bottle may be opened and used during the day, so buyers should understand how the body, cap and removable parts are meant to be cleaned. Request written care instructions for the exact model and compare them with customer information the retailer plans to publish. Do not infer dishwasher suitability, heat resistance or safe liquid temperature from a resin abbreviation, photo or different bottle. If the retailer expects repeated use, ask which components can be removed, how to reassemble them and whether replacement parts are available for the specified model. Have the review team follow the supplier's instructions on the sample and record unclear steps. This is an operational check, not a substitute for product-specific material documents or a market-compliance review.

sections.heading: 6. Compare capacity and user fit without turning size classes into claims
sections.paragraph: Keep stated milliliter capacity as the exact product record, then evaluate the filled sample in the customer's real carry context. Current product pages list model 2400 at 380 ml, model 2401 at 650 ml and model 2470 at 800 ml; their oz labels are approximate size classes. Compare these records and samples as different size choices, but do not infer weight, dimensions or use time from capacity alone. Record what was measured and where it came from. If the product page, approved sample and quote disagree, stop the reorder until the source is resolved. Use one row per model and cap configuration so the team can link test notes to the right SKU.

sections.heading: 7. Sign a sample approval production can follow
sections.paragraph: End the reorder decision with a dated approval connecting the test result to the production specification. List exact model, body and cap version, capacity, color, decoration, package, quantity, destination, care document and sample reference. Attach clear photos of the approved sample and any label or artwork. Record which tests were performed and avoid broader wording than the evidence supports. Ask the supplier to mark a substitution or design change before production; a verbal confirmation is difficult to compare during receipt inspection. Keep the approved file with the purchase order and use it again during reorder review. This gives purchasing, quality and merchandising one shared reference if a later delivery looks different.

checklist: Name the sports customer and activity the sample represents.
Record the exact model, cap and sample revision.
Follow supplier instructions and record each test condition.
Check cap opening and closing with the intended user.
Document leak checks without claiming a universal guarantee.
Measure dimensions against the real bag, cage or display.
Request model-specific cleaning and care instructions.
Compare exact ml and mark oz as an approximate size class.
Match test notes, product page, quote and purchase order.
Approve a dated sample reference and require written change control.

faqs.question: Can a retailer approve a bottle from a product photo?
faqs.answer: A photo can help shortlist a model, but it cannot verify cap handling, dimensions, cleaning steps or the assembled sample. Review the exact sample and keep a dated record before a bulk reorder.

faqs.question: Does one successful leak check guarantee the whole order?
faqs.answer: No. Record the sample and the conditions tested. Do not turn a limited check into a production-wide or all-use guarantee unless appropriate evidence supports that claim.

faqs.question: Should sports retailers test with the bottle full?
faqs.answer: Use a safe, controlled method consistent with manufacturer instructions and intended carry use. Record fill level, closure steps, orientation and inspection conditions so another reviewer can understand the result.

faqs.question: What documents should accompany a bulk sports-bottle reorder?
faqs.answer: Keep approved sample photos, exact model and cap version, capacity, color, artwork, package, care instructions, test notes and written confirmation of production changes.

title: Will a Reusable Water Bottle Fit Your Refill Station? A B2B Site-Test Checklist
description: A facility buyer's checklist to test bottle height, opening, cap clearance and refill workflow with the actual dispenser before ordering wholesale.
intro: A bottle that looks suitable in a catalog may be awkward at the facility's refill point. Before a school, gym, office or hospitality program orders in bulk, compare the exact assembled sample with the actual dispenser, counter and user workflow, then record the approved model and conditions.
coverAlt: A woman fills a clear bottle beneath a water pipe in an industrial setting; contextual Pexels photo, not an XUYI facility or test.
primary_keyword: reusable water bottle fit refill station wholesale buyer checklist
secondary_keywords: water bottle refill station compatibility test
bulk reusable bottle for office refill points
wholesale bottles for gyms and schools

sections.heading: 1. Identify the exact refill point and how people use it
sections.paragraph: Start with the equipment at the facility, not a generic idea of a water fountain. Record the dispenser or filling station make and model if available, where users stand, whether the space is public or staff-only, and whether people arrive with a cap, handle or strap attached. Observe the flow at the location: approach, position, filling, closing and moving away. A school corridor, gym floor, office kitchen and hotel service area may have different clearances and traffic. If more than one dispenser type is installed, test each relevant one or document which locations are outside the program. Do not infer compatibility from a bottle photo or equipment marketing name; the physical relationship between opening, nozzle, counter and user is what the facility must confirm.

sections.heading: 2. Measure the bottle and opening that will be used
sections.paragraph: Ask the supplier for exact external height, widest body diameter, cap height and mouth opening for the selected model, then verify the assembled sample. Measure from the base to the highest point of the cap because a handle or spout may change how the bottle sits under a nozzle. Record the mouth opening only when the supplier confirms the measurement point; nominal capacity does not describe the opening. Test with the intended cap fitted and note whether it must be removed during refill. Current XUYI pages list model 2400 at 380 ml, model 2401 at 650 ml and model 2470 at 800 ml, but those capacities do not establish nozzle clearance or opening dimensions. Compare the exact product record with the actual refill point.

sections.heading: 3. Test the selected sample at the real facility location
sections.paragraph: Bring the assembled sample to the location and follow the facility's normal procedure. Position it under the actual stream, check whether the rim or cap hits equipment, and observe whether the user can hold it steadily without blocking a control or surrounding traffic. Use a dry run first if the site requires it, then perform a normal water refill if safe and allowed. Record dispenser, sample model, cap state and reviewer. One successful demonstration establishes only that the tested combination worked in those conditions; it does not prove every dispenser or bottle variant is compatible. If users struggle to align the opening or remove the cap, record the issue and test another model or workflow before committing to a large order.

sections.heading: 4. Check the whole refill workflow, not only nozzle clearance
sections.paragraph: The facility needs to understand where the cap goes while the bottle is open, where users can set down a full bottle, and whether the location has enough space for a person to refill and leave without blocking others. If the bottle includes a removable strap or other part, confirm how it is handled at the refill point. Ask the site manager whether the floor, counter and cleaning arrangements create specific restrictions. Photograph the setup without identifiable people unless authorized. The purpose is to evaluate the real workflow and make a practical purchase decision, not to claim that a bottle works in every public station. Capture one approved setup for each distinct dispenser type and keep site notes with the sample record.

sections.heading: 5. Compare capacity, weight and refill frequency as a facility decision
sections.paragraph: Capacity is one input to facility selection. Use the exact milliliter capacity recorded for the model, then compare the filled sample's actual weight and dimensions in intended users' hands. A larger bottle may require fewer visits to a refill point but may be harder to carry for some users; do not state a universal preference without facility feedback. Ask the program owner how often people can refill, how the bottle will be stored and whether staff carry it between rooms. The catalog lists 380 ml for model 2400, 650 ml for 2401 and 800 ml for 2470; each page also gives an approximate oz class. Keep ml exact and treat oz as a size class, then let the site test determine which option works.

sections.heading: 6. Review material and care documents for the destination market
sections.paragraph: The physical refill check does not answer material or use-condition questions. Ask for written care instructions and model-specific documentation for the bottle body, cap, seal and each component contacting liquid. If the facility has rules for permitted materials, temperature, cleaning products or user groups, give them to the supplier before the quote is approved. For EU sales, the European Commission describes the food-contact framework and specific measures for plastic materials; U.S. buyers should check the applicable FDA regulatory status for each food-contact component. These official references explain market rules but do not certify a particular XUYI model. Tie each compliance statement to exact supplier evidence, finished product and intended conditions.

sections.heading: 7. Approve a site-tested model and keep the next order aligned
sections.paragraph: Close the decision with a short approval record: facility location, dispenser type, exact model, capacity, cap and body configuration, measured dimensions, refill steps, care document, color, decoration and sample photos. Name the person who approved the test and the date. If the program covers several sites, list which dispenser types were checked and which remain pending. Link the record to the purchase order so a later reorder can be compared with the same approved combination. A current product page is a starting SKU record, not evidence of site testing. Ask the manufacturer to flag any proposed change in cap, body, dimensions or material before production and repeat the relevant test if the change affects the refill workflow.

checklist: List every dispenser type and facility location covered.
Record exact model, cap and ml capacity.
Request and measure model-specific height, diameter and opening.
Test the assembled sample at the actual refill point.
Check cap removal, nozzle clearance, user position and traffic.
Record which sample and dispenser were tested and by whom.
Separate a single-site test from claims about all locations.
Review care instructions and market-specific material documents.
Save approved photos and site notes with the purchase order.
Recheck cap, body, dimensions or material changes before reorder.

faqs.question: Can a product listing confirm that a bottle fits a refill station?
faqs.answer: Usually it cannot establish fit by itself. Compare exact bottle measurements with the actual dispenser and test the assembled sample at the location where the program will operate.

faqs.question: Which bottle measurements matter most at a refill point?
faqs.answer: Check overall height with cap fitted, widest body diameter, the supplier-defined opening measurement, and any handle or strap that changes positioning. Confirm measurement points before comparing equipment clearance.

faqs.question: Should the cap stay on during refilling?
faqs.answer: That depends on the bottle design and workflow. Test the selected cap at the site, follow supplier instructions and record whether the cap must be removed and where it can be placed.

faqs.question: Does one successful test at one dispenser approve every site?
faqs.answer: No. The result applies to the tested model, cap, dispenser and conditions. For different equipment or layouts, record what was checked and test materially different setups.

title: What Should a Wholesale Water Bottle Purchase Order Say About Approved Samples and Substitutions?
description: A practical B2B guide to writing an approved-sample, component, packaging and substitution rule into a wholesale water bottle purchase order.
intro: A wholesale water bottle purchase order should do more than state a quantity and a unit price. It should identify the exact product configuration that was reviewed, show which sample and artwork were approved, and explain what happens if a supplier proposes a different lid, seal, material, color or package. Those details make the order easier to receive, compare and reorder. They also prevent a common dispute: the supplier believes a similar catalogue item is acceptable while the buyer believes the approved sample defines the goods. This guide turns that gap into a short, auditable purchase-order control.
coverAlt: Natural editorial photograph of reusable water bottle samples and an approval checklist on a buyer's worktable; not an exact XUYI product or factory inspection record.
primary_keyword: wholesale water bottle purchase order approved sample substitutions
secondary_keywords: approved sample purchase order water bottles

sections.heading: 1. Put the exact sellable configuration at the top of the order
sections.paragraph: Begin with an identity block that another buyer or receiving clerk can understand without opening a long email thread. Record the supplier model reference, the listed capacity, the bottle body, lid, seal, straw or strap components that belong to the order, the selected colorway and the intended packing format. Keep catalogue facts separate from open customization requests. For example, a 380 ml / 12 oz class reference, a 650 ml / 22 oz class reference and an 800 ml / 28 oz class reference are useful comparison points, but the purchase order still needs the exact SKU and assembled sample selected for production. Add the artwork revision, sample photo name and quotation revision to the same identity block. If a detail is not confirmed, mark it as pending instead of allowing a supplier or internal buyer to infer it from a product photograph. This simple header is the foundation for every later check.

sections.heading: 2. Define what the approved sample actually approves
sections.paragraph: The phrase approved sample is too vague unless the order explains what was examined. State whether approval covers the bottle body, closure operation, seal placement, drinking opening, decoration, color, dimensions, carton presentation or all of these items. Keep a dated photograph or physical sample reference with the purchase order, and record who approved it. If the sample was checked only for shape and appearance, do not let the order imply that it proves food-contact compliance, dishwasher performance, leak resistance or every production condition. Those claims require their own model-specific evidence and use conditions. A good order tells the supplier which characteristics are locked and which remain subject to a separate document or test. It also gives the receiving team a usable boundary: a different component is not automatically acceptable just because the finished bottle still looks similar.

sections.heading: 3. Write the substitution rule in plain operational language
sections.paragraph: A substitution clause should name the parts that cannot be changed silently: bottle body resin or grade, lid, gasket, straw, valve, handle, decoration process, color reference and individual or master packaging. Then state the approval sequence for a proposed change. The supplier should identify the affected SKU, explain why the change is needed, provide the revised material or component information, show a representative sample and wait for written buyer approval before mass production or shipment. Avoid a sentence such as equivalent material may be used unless equivalence is defined by the buyer's intended market, use conditions, dimensions, function and documentation. A lower-cost or more available component may still alter cleaning access, fit, appearance, printed area or customer instructions. The goal is not to prevent every engineering change; it is to stop an unrecorded change from becoming a receiving dispute.

sections.heading: 4. Connect artwork, color and packing to the same order revision
sections.paragraph: Many wholesale problems happen because product approval and packaging approval live in different files. Link the bottle sample to the artwork proof, body and lid color references, label language, carton marks, inner packing and master-carton instruction. If the order contains several colors or capacities, list each variant separately and show its quantity, image or sample reference and internal item code. Do not rely on a single group photograph to define every variant. If a logo position, color, carton label or insert changes after the sample is approved, update the order revision and state whether a new physical sample is required. The receiving team should be able to compare a carton label with the purchase order and identify the variant without guessing. This is particularly important for private-label and distributor orders, where a visually small change can create a different retail item or a different customer promise.

sections.heading: 5. Make receiving evidence part of the purchase-order plan
sections.paragraph: A purchase order is more useful when it tells the buyer what to record when goods arrive. Define the receiving checks for the exact model, quantity, visible finish, lid and seal assembly, artwork version, colorway, packing unit and carton identification. If a functional test is required, write the method and conditions that the buyer will actually use; do not insert a generic word such as leakproof without a defined procedure. Keep the receiving record tied to the purchase-order revision, sample reference and lot or carton information. Separate critical issues that stop release from minor observations that can be corrected or documented. This does not mean the buyer is claiming that every unit was tested. It means the order creates a repeatable record of what was checked, what was not checked and which party must resolve a mismatch before the goods enter the sales channel.

sections.heading: 6. State the reapproval triggers before production starts
sections.paragraph: List the changes that require a new sample or written approval before the supplier proceeds: a different body or lid material, a new closure component, a changed seal, a new mold or cavity, a different decoration method, a color reference change, a capacity or dimension change, a new packaging format and any change that affects the destination-market documentation. Also state what happens if the supplier discovers a production constraint after approval. The buyer may accept a documented alternative, request another sample or cancel the affected line, but the decision should be recorded against the same order revision. Do not make the supplier guess whether an apparently small change is material to the buyer. A short trigger list is easier to follow than a general promise to maintain quality, and it gives both sides a clear point at which a new comparison is required.

sections.heading: 7. Leave a reorder record that another colleague can use
sections.paragraph: Close the order with a handoff package: the final quotation, approved sample identifier, product and component list, artwork and color records, packing instruction, receiving checklist, open deviations and the contact responsible for change approval. Save the package using the supplier model and internal variant code rather than a vague campaign name. When the next order is prepared, compare the new quotation against the prior approved configuration and ask the supplier to confirm whether any component, material, decoration or packaging has changed. If the program adds a new capacity or color, create a new variant record instead of editing the old one until the difference is approved. This makes the order history useful for procurement, quality, sales and customer service. A good purchase order is not only a legal or commercial document; it is the smallest reliable source of truth for the next reorder.

checklist: Record the exact supplier model, capacity and assembled configuration.
Attach the dated sample reference and identify who approved it.
List bottle, lid, seal, straw, handle, decoration and packing components.
Require written notice and sample review before a substitution or change.
Separate catalogue facts from custom material and compliance requests.
Give every color, capacity and package variant its own order line.
Tie artwork, color references and carton labels to the same revision.
Define receiving checks and any functional test conditions in plain language.
List the changes that trigger a new sample or written approval.
Save the final order package so the next reorder can be compared line by line.

faqs.question: Is an approved water bottle sample enough to accept a bulk shipment?
faqs.answer: It is a reference point, not proof that every unit was tested. Compare the received model, components, appearance, packing and any agreed functional checks with the approved sample and record the result.

faqs.question: Can a supplier replace a bottle lid with an equivalent part?
faqs.answer: Only after the buyer reviews the affected function, dimensions, materials, care information and destination-market evidence. Similar appearance does not establish equivalence.

faqs.question: What should a private-label bottle purchase order identify?
faqs.answer: Identify the exact model, capacity, body and lid components, colorway, artwork revision, packing, carton marks, sample reference, receiving checks and change-approval rule.

faqs.question: When should a new water bottle sample be requested?
faqs.answer: Request one when a body, lid, seal, straw, material, mold, decoration, color, capacity, dimension or packaging change could affect the approved configuration or the buyer's claims.

es.category: CONTROL DE PEDIDOS AL POR MAYOR
es.title: ¿Qué debe indicar una orden mayorista de botellas sobre muestras aprobadas y sustituciones?
es.description: Guía B2B para fijar en la orden la muestra aprobada, los componentes, el embalaje y el procedimiento para cualquier sustitución.
es.intro: Una orden mayorista de botellas de agua debe hacer más que indicar cantidad y precio. Tiene que identificar la configuración exacta revisada, enlazar la muestra y el arte aprobados y explicar qué ocurre si el proveedor propone otra tapa, junta, material, color o envase. Así la recepción y la reposición se pueden auditar sin depender de una cadena de correos.
sections: 1. Coloque la configuración vendible exacta al inicio de la orden

Comience con un bloque de identidad que otro comprador o responsable de recepción pueda entender sin abrir correos antiguos. Registre modelo, capacidad, cuerpo, tapa, junta, pajita o asa, color y embalaje. Separe datos de catálogo y personalización pendiente. Añada la revisión del arte, la foto de la muestra y la versión de la cotización. Si un dato no está confirmado, márquelo como pendiente y no permita que se deduzca de una fotografía.
2. Defina qué aprueba realmente la muestra

La expresión muestra aprobada es demasiado amplia si no dice qué se revisó. Indique si cubre cuerpo, cierre, junta, abertura, decoración, color, dimensiones, caja o el conjunto. Guarde fecha, fotos y persona aprobadora. Una muestra visual no demuestra por sí sola contacto alimentario, lavavajillas o estanqueidad. Separe las características bloqueadas de los documentos o pruebas independientes.
3. Escriba la regla de sustitución con lenguaje operativo

Nombre las piezas que no se pueden cambiar en silencio: cuerpo, resina, tapa, junta, pajita, válvula, asa, decoración, color y embalaje. El proveedor debe indicar la pieza, el motivo, la información revisada y una muestra representativa, y esperar aprobación escrita. Una pieza parecida no es automáticamente equivalente si cambia limpieza, ajuste, apariencia o instrucciones.
4. Una el arte, el color y el embalaje a la misma revisión

Relacione la muestra con el arte, los colores del cuerpo y la tapa, la etiqueta, el idioma, el embalaje interior y las marcas de la caja. Si hay varios colores o capacidades, cada variante debe tener línea, cantidad, imagen o muestra y código interno. No use una sola foto de grupo para definir todas las combinaciones.
5. Convierta la recepción en parte del plan de compra

Defina qué registrar al llegar: modelo, cantidad, acabado, tapa y junta, versión del arte, color, unidad de embalaje y caja. Si existe una prueba funcional, escriba condiciones y criterio. Vincule el registro a la revisión, muestra y lote, sin afirmar que se probó cada unidad. Separe problemas que bloquean la liberación de observaciones menores.
6. Fije los disparadores de reaprobación antes de producir

Liste los cambios que requieren nueva muestra o aprobación: cuerpo o tapa, material, junta, pajita, molde, decoración, color, capacidad, medidas o embalaje. Si aparece una limitación, el comprador puede aceptar una alternativa documentada, pedir otra muestra o detener la línea. Una lista breve funciona mejor que una promesa general de calidad.
7. Deje un expediente que sirva para la próxima reposición

Cierre con cotización, muestra, componentes, arte, colores, embalaje, recepción, desviaciones y responsable. Guárdelo por modelo y código de variante. En la siguiente compra compare la cotización con esa configuración y pregunte qué cambió. Así compras, calidad, ventas y servicio usan la misma evidencia.
checklist: Modelo, capacidad y configuración ensamblada exactos.
Referencia fechada de la muestra y persona aprobadora.
Cuerpo, tapa, junta, pajita, asa, decoración y embalaje.
Aviso y revisión antes de cualquier sustitución.
Datos de catálogo separados de solicitudes de material o cumplimiento.
Cada color, capacidad y paquete en su propia línea.
Arte, colores y marcas de caja unidos a la revisión.
Pruebas de recepción y condiciones escritas con claridad.
Cambios que disparan nueva muestra o aprobación.
Expediente final guardado para comparar la reposición.
faqs: ¿Una muestra aprobada basta para aceptar un envío mayorista?
Es una referencia, no la prueba de cada unidad. Compare modelo, componentes, apariencia, embalaje y pruebas acordadas y registre el resultado.
¿Puede el proveedor cambiar la tapa por una pieza equivalente?
Solo después de revisar función, dimensiones, materiales, cuidados y evidencia del mercado. La apariencia parecida no prueba equivalencia.
¿Qué debe identificar una orden de botellas de marca privada?
Modelo, capacidad, componentes, color, arte, embalaje, marcas de caja, muestra, recepción y regla de cambios.
¿Cuándo se debe pedir una nueva muestra?
Cuando cuerpo, tapa, junta, pajita, material, molde, decoración, color, capacidad, dimensiones o embalaje puedan cambiar la configuración.

pt.title: O que um pedido atacadista deve dizer sobre amostras aprovadas e substituições?
pt.description: Guia B2B para registrar no pedido a amostra aprovada, os componentes, a embalagem e o processo para qualquer substituição.
pt.intro: Um pedido atacadista de garrafas de água deve fazer mais do que indicar quantidade e preço. Ele precisa identificar a configuração exata revisada, ligar a amostra e a arte aprovadas ao pedido e explicar o que acontece se o fornecedor propuser outra tampa, vedação, material, cor ou embalagem. Assim, recebimento e reposição podem ser auditados sem depender de uma sequência de e-mails.
sections: 1. Coloque a configuração vendável no início do pedido

Comece com um bloco de identidade que outro comprador entenda sem abrir mensagens antigas. Registre modelo, capacidade, corpo, tampa, vedação, canudo ou alça, cores e embalagem. Separe fatos de catálogo das opções de personalização abertas. Inclua revisão da arte, referência da amostra e versão da cotação. Dado não confirmado deve ficar pendente, não ser uma suposição.
2. Defina o que a amostra realmente aprova

A expressão amostra aprovada é ampla demais se o pedido não disser o que foi examinado. Indique corpo, fechamento, vedação, abertura, decoração, cor, dimensões, caixa ou conjunto. Guarde data, fotos e responsável. A amostra visual não prova sozinha contato com alimentos, lava-louças ou vedação. Separe características bloqueadas de documentos e testes independentes.
3. Escreva a regra de substituição claramente

Nomeie as peças que não podem mudar em silêncio: corpo, resina, tampa, vedação, canudo, válvula, alça, decoração, cor e embalagem. O fornecedor deve indicar a peça, o motivo, a informação revisada e uma amostra, aguardando aprovação escrita. Aparência semelhante não significa equivalência se mudar limpeza, encaixe, aparência ou instruções.
4. Ligue arte, cor e embalagem à mesma revisão

Relacione a amostra à arte, cores do corpo e tampa, rótulo, idioma, embalagem interna e marcas da caixa. Para várias cores ou capacidades, cada variante precisa de linha, quantidade, imagem ou amostra e código interno. Uma foto de grupo não define todas as combinações.
5. Faça do recebimento parte do plano de compra

Defina o registro de modelo, quantidade, acabamento, tampa e vedação, arte, cor, unidade e caixa. Para teste funcional, escreva condições e critério. Ligue o registro à revisão, amostra e lote, sem dizer que cada unidade foi testada. Separe falhas que bloqueiam a liberação de observações menores.
6. Defina os gatilhos de nova aprovação

Liste mudanças em corpo, tampa, material, vedação, canudo, molde, decoração, cor, capacidade, medidas ou embalagem que exigem nova amostra ou aprovação. Se surgir uma limitação, o comprador pode aceitar alternativa documentada, pedir outra amostra ou parar a linha. Uma lista curta é melhor que promessa genérica.
7. Deixe um arquivo útil para a próxima reposição

Feche o pedido com cotação, amostra, componentes, arte, cores, embalagem, recebimento, desvios e responsável. Guarde por modelo e código de variante. Na compra seguinte compare a cotação com essa configuração e pergunte o que mudou. Compras, qualidade, vendas e atendimento passam a usar a mesma evidência.
checklist: Modelo, capacidade e configuração montada exatos.
Referência datada da amostra e responsável.
Corpo, tampa, vedação, canudo, alça, decoração e embalagem.
Aviso e revisão antes de substituição.
Fatos de catálogo separados de solicitações de material ou conformidade.
Cada cor, capacidade e pacote em sua linha.
Arte, cores e marcas de caixa ligadas à revisão.
Testes de recebimento e condições escritos.
Mudanças que exigem nova amostra ou aprovação.
Arquivo final guardado para a reposição.
faqs: Uma amostra aprovada basta para aceitar um lote atacadista?
É uma referência, não prova de cada unidade. Compare modelo, componentes, aparência, embalagem e testes acordados e registre o resultado.
O fornecedor pode substituir a tampa por uma peça equivalente?
Somente após revisar função, dimensões, materiais, cuidados e evidências do destino. Aparência parecida não prova equivalência.
O que um pedido de garrafas de marca própria deve identificar?
Modelo, capacidade, componentes, cor, arte, embalagem, marcas da caixa, amostra, recebimento e regra de mudança.
Quando pedir nova amostra?
Quando corpo, tampa, vedação, canudo, material, molde, decoração, cor, capacidade, dimensões ou embalagem puderem mudar a configuração.
